summary: TeleportXR is a session protocol, not a document format. A server runs the live simulation and holds the truth of it; each client receives only the partial, temporary slice of state it needs right now. Three transports run in parallel: a WebSocket for signalling, WebRTC data channels and media tracks for real-time data and audio, and plain HTTP for static assets. Its own documentation states that Teleport has no file format and that the Teleport network is part of the Internet but not part of the Web. It is by some distance the most completely specified subject in this group at the session layer, and it is the only one here that states its unit: linear units are metres, and handedness and vertical axis are negotiated rather than assumed. Between 2026-06-16 and 2026-09-03 the identity gap that used to define this subject was largely filled, in the reference implementations first and the specification second. An avatar offer may now carry the address of a signed Universal Manifest instead of a bare asset URL; the server verifies Ed25519 over RFC 8785 canonical JSON, gates each facet against the subject's own consent records with default-deny, and returns a structured receipt. Separately the connect message's identity member, still documented as an opaque string, is implemented as a structured identity with three trust levels and a challenge-response that binds an OpenID Connect token to a client-held key. Three cautions. The chapter that would specify the manifest mechanism, avatar_manifest, is referenced from three places and is not in the public repository. Verification is explicitly not proof of the bearer's right to the document, and only trust tier zero is supported. And watch the word Node: a TeleportXR node is a changing object inside a live stream with no URL, which is not what the same word means in a world-addressing API.

coverage.note: Three layers in parallel: a WebSocket for signalling, WebRTC by default for real-time streams with optional legacy SRT and EFP, and HTTP or HTTPS for static assets. Reliable payloads must work over either the WebSocket or the WebRTC reliable channel and receivers must accept both for the whole session. One caution for an implementer: the normative channel table says five SCTP data channels and three other places in the same documentation set say six, so the count is not settled in the text; channels are matched by label, and five labels are defined.

coverage.note: A full connection state machine with four named phases, reconnection, timeouts and an enumerated state list. The client repeats a connect message until it gets a response carrying a client and server identifier as unsigned 64-bit numbers; a matching server identifier lets cached resource and node identifiers persist across a reconnect, though the client may not assume it. Authentication of the asset service is still deliberately outside the protocol: the HTTP service is shared by every connected client with no per-client authentication. Since 2026-06-16 the reference implementations have added a session-level identity handshake on the signalling channel, which the protocol document does not yet describe; see identity.root.

coverage.note: Time is in microseconds. The setup command carries the session start as a server wall-clock value in Unix time and every other time on the wire is an offset from it, with a ping and pong pair for latency. The limit is stated plainly: the client's own session-relative timestamps are monotonic within one session and are not comparable across clients or to any wall clock, so this is a session clock rather than a shared ordering guarantee between participants.

coverage.note: Presence is inferred from the scene, not announced. Another client arrives as an ordinary node on the geometry channel, and a voice arrives as an audio track whose session-description identifier is the decimal uid of the node that emits it. The protocol states outright that no signalling message tells a client anything about another client's avatar, and that client identifiers are never exposed to other clients. Two earlier claims in this row have been retracted: the peer message form and the audio participant state change command are both withdrawn upstream, and the command identifiers for AudioSourceMapping and AudioParticipantStateChange are now reserved with servers forbidden to send them.

coverage.note: The protocol states outright that Teleport has no file format, and that the Teleport network is part of the Internet but not part of the Web. A node here is a changing object inside a live stream with no URL, not addressable from outside the session, where a world-addressing API means a fetchable, editable record by the same name. coverage.note: Handedness and vertical axis are negotiated rather than assumed. The client declares its native axes in the handshake, the server publishes the axes its scene is authored in, and every server-to-client packet carrying geometry is already converted into the client's standard. The standard is a one-byte value with four complete named combinations and discriminator bits so that no two are the same byte, and a server must support at least the engineering and OpenGL styles. Assets fetched over HTTP are the exception: they are served as authored and the pointer chunk declares which frame they are in, so the client converts. Transforms are local to the parent, and a root node is expressed directly in the server's global space.

In a room session the server is a selective forwarding unit: each microphone arrives on one inbound track and a chosen subset is forwarded to every other listener as separate outbound tracks, with loopback suppression required and hysteresis recommended before a speaker is dropped from a listener's set.

coverage.note: Positioning a sound is now a single rule and it is a good one: the outbound track's session-description identifier is set to the decimal uid of the node that emits the sound, and that is the only binding between the audio transport and the scene. Identifier zero, or one naming a node the client cannot place, plays without position, so an announcer or a music bed needs no node. Because that identifier cannot change for the life of a media line, the binding is stable for the whole session. The earlier claim in this row, that an audio source mapping command binds streams to places, is withdrawn: that command is now reserved and servers must not send it.

coverage.note: Input is negotiated rather than fixed. The server declares the inputs it expects as a list of identifier, type and path, where the path is a regular expression matched against the client's own control paths, and the client decides which physical control satisfies each one. A new declaration replaces the previous set wholesale and invalidates every earlier identifier.

sources.quote: ``path`` is a regular expression matched against the client-side control path (e.g. ``"/user/hand/left/input/trigger/value"`` on OpenXR). The client decides which physical control satisfies each regex; multiple controls may match, in which case the client picks one.

coverage.note: Two mechanisms exist and one of them is empty. The server does tell the client which control inputs it expects, and the client declares its axes standard in the handshake, so the parts that matter for drawing and for input do flow. But the general capability bag on the connect message has no defined keys at all: it is an extension point with a rule that unknown keys must be ignored, and the conventions chapter says plainly that there is no formal capability negotiation beyond the rendering features flag and the session-description exchange. This row was previously scored native; that overstated it.

sources.quote: ``capabilities`` (optional) is a free-form object advertising optional protocol features supported by the client. Unknown keys MUST be ignored, so the set can grow without a version bump. No keys are currently defined; the member is the extension point for future signaling-level capabilities.

sources.title: TeleportXR conventions.rst (teleportxr/Teleport, main)

coverage.note: Avatars are negotiated rather than defined, and the negotiation has grown teeth since 2026-06-16. The server advertises a policy; the reference structure for that policy now carries first-class limits for accepted formats, file size, triangle count, height and width in metres, texture count and total texture pixels, a named skeleton, and a list of allowed licence tags. The client offers a URL with a declared format and byte count, and the server accepts or refuses and says whether delivery is by relay or by import. A relayed URL must end in a recognised extension because clients pick a decoder by extension; the extensions named are glTF binary, VRM and glTF. The avatar file's own contents remain out of scope.

sources.title: TeleportXR signaling.rst (teleportxr/Teleport, main)
sources.quote: A relayed URL must end in a recognised asset extension (``.glb``, ``.vrm``, ``.gltf``), since clients select a decoder by extension.

coverage.note: This is the row that changed most since 2026-06-16, and it is the single most consequential change in the subject. An avatar offer may now name a signed Universal Manifest instead of a bare asset address, and the server reads the asset address out of the verified manifest. The reference server ships the resolver, verifies Signature Profile A (Ed25519 over RFC 8785 canonical JSON with the signature member removed), gates every facet by the subject's own consent records with default-deny, caches on the manifest's own expiry rather than the HTTP response, and returns a structured receipt to the client saying what it did with the document. Two limits are stated by the implementers themselves and both matter: only trust tier zero, signature-only, is actually verified, and verification deliberately does not check that the manifest's subject is the client presenting it, so a verified manifest is authentic but not proof of the bearer's right to it. The older empty proof registry is still there in the signalling document, and mid-session revocation remains real.

coverage.note: The published protocol document and the reference implementations no longer agree, and an implementer should know which one they are building against. The signalling chapter still says the identity member is an opaque string supplied for application-level authentication that may be empty. Both reference servers now treat that bare string as a legacy shape and accept an object with a provider, an issuer, a subject and a display name, sorted into three trust levels: anonymous, asserted, and verified. Asserted gets its own keyspace precisely because anyone can claim anyone's subject; verified keys derive only from the token's own claims and never from anything the client typed. Two new signalling message types, identity-challenge and identity-response, carry the freshness proof. None of this is in the protocol document.

coverage.note: This row was scored none and that is no longer true. The reference server now has a credential verification registry keyed by credential type, with a named list of the schemes a server might accept: an OpenID Connect identity token, a plain OAuth2 access token, a W3C verifiable credential or decentralized identifier proof, and a SAML assertion. One of the four is implemented; the rest are left to host applications. The implemented one is careful: the identity token is bound to a long-lived client key by putting the key's thumbprint in the token's nonce, and a live challenge-response proves the presenter holds that key, so a token captured by one server cannot be replayed at another. TeleportXR still defines no credential format of its own. An earlier claim in this row, that the words consent, trust, permission, provenance, encryption and credential were all absent from the project, no longer holds and is withdrawn.

An avatar offer and a peer relay carry a content hash beside the URL so a peer can check it fetched the file the owner meant. Separately the client's asset cache is keyed by URL, and the specification places the obligation on the server: publish each immutable asset at a unique, stable URL. coverage.note: Assets come over ordinary HTTP but the protocol explicitly pushes the usual web delivery machinery outside itself: resource expiry, entity tag handling, range requests and authentication are all stated as not part of the protocol, and the service is shared by every client. That collides with a world-addressing standard in the same stack whose asset pillar is built out of exactly those things, entity tags, conditional requests and per-request authorisation. Two specifications a client would have to satisfy at once take opposite positions on whether HTTP caching semantics are in scope.

coverage.note: The protocol says where a sound is and refuses to say how it should reach the ears. A track bound to a placed node is spatialised by the client at that node's world transform, and the layering is explicit: the server decides whether a listener receives a track, the client decides how loud. Gain and rolloff are client or application defaults and are deliberately not carried on the wire, so two conformant clients in the same room may attenuate the same voice differently. There is no head-related transfer function, no ambisonic model, no room acoustics and no occlusion.

coverage.note: Permission is read, not defined. Where a deployment turns on the manifest option, the server evaluates the subject's own consent records before it uses any part of the document, and the rule is default-deny: a facet with no consent entry naming it is recorded as consent-missing and its data must not be processed. The exception is deliberate and stated: an unstated reference is permitted for the avatar pointer itself, because consent in that model is defined over facets and demanding one per pointer would reject every manifest in circulation. coverage.note: There is no agent inside the world, but since 2026-06-16 there is a documented way for one to drive a client from outside. A headless client runs as a daemon and a line-oriented control protocol on a loopback socket lets a terminal, a script, a continuous-integration job or a language-model agent issue one command and read one response. It is explicitly not the streaming protocol and it has no authentication, on the stated ground that anything able to open a loopback socket already has the user's shell. Nothing in the world protocol distinguishes a person from a program.

Logic stays on the server; the client is given geometry and video. Nothing is published as a unit of logic under a name that another author would depend on.
A remote rendering protocol carries frames between one server and one client it has already connected to. There is no publishing path to an audience in which a review could stand.
The protocol has no geographic frame and no map of a real place.
A server is found by an out-of-band address, not by the region it covers, and it declares no area of application.
